358.title: When a neighbor's cup breaks
358.hook: when someone else's cup breaks we say "these things happen," so say it of your own (Enchiridion 26)
358.tomorrow: A target isn't set up to be missed
358.howItsDone: Some Stoic practitioners treat their own setbacks the way they would a friend's, using the same calm words they would readily offer someone else.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the price of lettuce. Your line was I kept the coin. Did you notice a price you didn't pay, and what you kept? Day three hundred fifty-eight.
screen: `THE PRICE OF LETTUCE — I KEPT THE COIN.`

segments.voice: A friend texts: I dented my car backing out of the garage. Your reply takes four seconds. Oh no! Happens to everyone. Is anyone hurt? That's what matters. Wise, calm, kind. A week later you dent your own car backing out of your own garage, and for the next hour you're a different person. Idiot. How could I. This always happens to me. Same kind of dent. Same kind of morning. Somehow you had perfect perspective for your friend and none at all for yourself. Section twenty-six of the handbook says the wisdom you need was in that four-second text. Today: when a neighbor's cup breaks.
screen: `A FRIEND'S DENTED CAR.` → `HAPPENS TO EVERYONE.` → `THEN IT'S YOUR CAR.`

segments.voice: First, the method. What nature intends, Epictetus says, we can learn from the cases where we all agree. Not from arguments. From our own easy answers about other people's troubles. Second, the cup. When someone else's servant breaks a cup, we're quick to say: these things happen. So, he says, when your own cup breaks, be the same as you were when the other one broke. That's all. Borrow your own good advice. Third, bigger things. Then he carries it further, gently but firmly. When someone else's child or spouse dies, everyone says: that's the human lot. But when it's one's own, right away it's: oh, poor me, how wretched. We ought to remember, he says, how we felt when we heard the same news about others. Here it's worth slowing down, because this is a hard line to hear. Epictetus asks a great deal: the same steadiness for your own loss as for a stranger's. Not every reader will follow him that far, and nobody here is asked to. But the part anyone can use is narrower. It's the doubled suffering, the sense that this, unlike everyone else's, shouldn't have happened, that the world has made an exception of you. Fourth, the practice under it. Often the wise, steady friend who knows exactly what to say about broken cups is already in the room. It's us, talking to someone else. The trick is to turn around and say it to ourselves, with the same warmth. It's strangely close to the old rule about loving your neighbor as yourself, only running backward. Treat yourself, for a moment, as you'd treat your neighbor. These things happen. To them. To you.

segments.voice: Bring to mind one trouble of your own that's been weighing on you. Something manageable: a mistake, a breakage, a bad week. Now imagine a friend telling you that exact story, as if it happened to them. Listen to them. What would you say? Let the words come, kind and steady. Then turn them around and say them to yourself, in the same tone. These things happen. Stay with that. The bell holds the time.
When a neighbor's cup breaks. Epictetus' mirror: the calm you have for other people's troubles is the wisdom to use on your own. Today's word.
screen: `WHEN A NEIGHBOR'S CUP BREAKS — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: these things happen. When something of yours breaks today, say what you'd say to a friend, and mean it for yourself. Day three hundred fifty-eight.

359.title: A target isn't set up to be missed
359.word: A target isn't set up to be missed
359.hook: evil isn't built into nature, any more than a target is set up to be missed (Enchiridion 27)
359.howItsDone: Some Stoic practitioners treat mistakes as misses rather than proof that the good is out of reach, and choose a specific good to aim at each day.

segments.voice: Yesterday: when a neighbor's cup breaks. Your line was these things happen. Did you say to yourself what you'd say to a friend? Day three hundred fifty-nine.

At an archery range, the targets stand in a row. Straw bales, painted rings, a gold circle in the middle. Some arrows land in the gold. Many land in the outer rings, or the grass, or the fence behind. But nobody hangs a target hoping it will be missed. The whole thing exists to be hit. The misses are real, sometimes there are lots of them, but they aren't what the target is for. Section twenty-seven of the handbook is a single sentence built on that picture, and a puzzling one. Today: a target isn't set up to be missed.
screen: `AN ARCHERY RANGE.` → `ARROWS IN THE GRASS.` → `NOBODY HANGS A TARGET TO BE MISSED.`

segments.voice: First, the sentence. Just as a target isn't set up in order to be missed, Epictetus says, so the nature of evil doesn't arise in the world. That's all he says. No example, no explanation. Second, the honest part. Readers still argue about this line, and nobody can be sure exactly what he meant. Here are two readings that have lasted. One, from the ancient commentator Simplicius and others: the world is ordered toward the good, the way a target is set up to be hit. Evil isn't one of its built-in parts. It's a missing, a falling short, real but not the point. Two, a more practical reading: in the world outside us, nothing is truly evil, because the only real evil, for a Stoic, is a bad choice in our own will. Either way, the picture says that the mark is there to be aimed at. Third, the word. The Greek for target is skopos, the mark an archer fixes the eye on. Notice what the picture does. It doesn't deny the misses; the grass behind a range is full of arrows. It says the misses aren't the reason the target is there. A miss only counts as a miss because there's a mark to measure it by. Fourth, what to do with it. Whatever the metaphysics, the practice is simple. A miss doesn't mean the target was a lie. Yesterday's sharp word, last week's broken promise: those are arrows in the grass. The gold is still there. Pick up another arrow. Aim at the good.
screen: `NOT SET UP TO BE MISSED.` · `TWO READINGS, NO CERTAINTY.` · `SKOPOS: THE MARK.` · `PICK UP ANOTHER ARROW.` · then, large: `AIM AT THE GOOD.`

segments.voice: Picture a target in front of you, the gold circle clear in the middle. Now name one good thing you could aim at today. Small and specific: a patient answer, a finished task, a kind word to someone who's hard to like. Put that in the gold. Remember one recent miss, and let it lie in the grass without picking it up to examine it. Then breathe in, and draw back an imaginary bow toward today's gold. The bell holds the time.
A target isn't set up to be missed. Epictetus' one-line picture: the world is made for aiming at the good; misses are real, but they aren't the point. Today's word.
screen: `A TARGET ISN'T SET UP TO BE MISSED — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: aim at the good. Choose one good to aim at today, and if you miss, pick up another arrow. Day three hundred fifty-nine.

360.title: Who handed you over?
360.hook: you'd be furious if someone handed your body to a stranger, so why hand your mind to anyone who insults you? (Enchiridion 28)
360.howItsDone: Some Stoic practitioners notice when another person's words have taken over their thoughts, and deliberately return their attention to their own judgment.

segments.voice: Yesterday: a target isn't set up to be missed. Your line was aim at the good. Did you choose one good to aim at, and pick up another arrow after a miss? Day three hundred sixty.

You're waiting at a bus stop when the person next to you takes your house keys out of your hand and gives them to a stranger walking past. Take care of these, they say. You'd be on your feet. You'd chase the stranger down the block. Nobody gets to hand over your keys. A different afternoon. A stranger in a comment section says something nasty about you. And for the next three hours, that stranger decides what you think about, how you feel, what you say at dinner. You handed them the keys yourself. Today: who handed you over?
screen: `YOUR KEYS, HANDED TO A STRANGER.` → `A NASTY COMMENT.` → `THREE HOURS, GIVEN AWAY.`

segments.voice: First, the comparison. If someone handed your body over to whoever happened to meet you, Epictetus says, you'd be indignant. Second, the turn. But you hand over your own mind to anyone you happen to meet, so that if they abuse you, it's shaken and thrown into confusion. Aren't you ashamed of that? He's blunt here. The word for mind here is gnome: your judgment, your way of thinking, the place you decide from. Third, how this differs from the insult, a little over a week ago. That day was about the moment of sting, and putting a breath between the sting and the reply. This is about ownership. Who is allowed into the control room? A stranger can say anything; that isn't up to you. But whether their words get the keys, whether they get to sit in your mind for the afternoon and steer, Epictetus thinks that part is yours to decide. Fourth, keeping the keys. It doesn't mean never being affected. A cruel word will land; you're not stone. It means noticing when you've stopped thinking your own thoughts and started running someone else's script. The replay in the shower. The imaginary argument on the commute. The urge to check if they've said more. When you catch it, you can ask Epictetus' question, a little amused at yourself: who handed you over? And then, gently, take the keys back. My mind is mine. There's something dignified in that. Not proud. Just a person who knows where their own house is, and doesn't leave the door open for anyone who happens by.
screen: `YOUR BODY, HANDED TO A STRANGER?` · `YOUR MIND, HANDED TO ANYONE.` · `GNOME: WHERE YOU DECIDE FROM.` · `TAKE THE KEYS BACK.` · then, large: `MY MIND IS MINE.`

segments.voice: Notice who is in your mind right now, besides you. Maybe a person from an argument, a voice from the news, a comment you read this morning. Picture them sitting at your desk, inside your head, steering. Don't fight them. Just see them clearly. Then, politely, picture yourself walking them to the door, thanking them, and closing it. Take your seat again. Feel your own breath, your own thoughts, your own quiet. The bell holds the time.
Who handed you over? Epictetus' question for a mind given away: we'd never hand a stranger our body, so why our judgment? Today's word.
Your line: my mind is mine. When you catch yourself replaying someone's words today, ask who handed you over, and take the keys back. Day three hundred sixty.

361.title: Count the cost first
361.hook: before you begin anything, look at what comes first and what follows, like an athlete before the games (Enchiridion 29)
361.howItsDone: Some Stoic practitioners, before taking on something new, picture its demands and setbacks in detail and only then decide whether to begin.

segments.voice: Yesterday: who handed you over? Your line was my mind is mine. When someone's words started steering, did you take the keys back? Day three hundred sixty-one.
screen: `WHO HANDED YOU OVER? — MY MIND IS MINE.`

segments.voice: New running shoes, still in the box. A water bottle with the hours printed down the side. A plan taped to the fridge. A few weeks later, the shoes are in the closet. The wanting didn't stop. The plan was all beginning and no middle: nobody pictured the five-forty alarm in the dark, the sore knees, the Thursday that didn't feel like it. Section twenty-nine of the handbook is about that missing middle, and it uses an athlete to show it. Today: count the cost first.
screen: `NEW SHOES, STILL IN THE BOX.` → `A FEW WEEKS LATER: THE CLOSET.` → `ALL BEGINNING, NO MIDDLE.`

segments.voice: First, the rule. In every undertaking, Epictetus says, look at what comes before it and what follows from it, and only then set about it. Otherwise you'll start eagerly, because you haven't thought about what comes next, and later, when some hard parts show up, you'll give up in shame. Second, the athlete. You want to win at Olympia? So do I, he says, it's a fine thing. But look at what comes first and what follows. You'll have to keep to a strict routine, eat on a schedule, stay off sweets, train at set hours in heat and cold, drink no cold water and no wine when you're told not to, hand yourself over to the trainer as to a doctor. Then in the contest you may dislocate a wrist, twist an ankle, swallow a lot of dust, take a beating, and after all that, lose. Third, the children. If you don't count the cost, he says, you'll be like children who play wrestlers, then gladiators, then trumpeters, then actors, trying everything and finishing nothing. Weigh it all, and then, if you still want it, go ahead. Fourth, a neighbor. The same picture appears in the Gospel of Luke, about following Jesus, in the King James words: "For which of you, intending to build a tower, sitteth not down first, and counteth the cost, whether he have sufficient to finish it?" A different teacher, a different calling, the same sitting down before you start. Epictetus' point isn't to scare anyone off. It's that people who have already seen the middle are better placed to get through it. Count it, and if you still want it, begin.
screen: `WHAT COMES FIRST, WHAT FOLLOWS.` · `THE ATHLETE: DIET, DUST, A BEATING.` · `LIKE CHILDREN TRYING EVERYTHING.` · `SIT DOWN FIRST, AND COUNT.` · then, large: `FIRST, WHAT FOLLOWS.`

segments.voice: Choose one plan you're about to start. A project, a habit, a trip, a hard conversation. Picture the beginning: it's easy to see. Now walk forward into the middle. What will the third week ask of you? What will you give up? Where will it get boring, or hard, or embarrassing? See it plainly, the way Epictetus lists the dust and the twisted ankle. Then, at the end, ask: do I still want it? Notice the answer. The bell holds the time.
Count the cost first. Epictetus' rule for every undertaking: look at what comes before and what follows, like an athlete before the games, then begin. Today's word.
Your line: first, what follows. Before you say yes to anything new today, take one minute to picture the middle. Day three hundred sixty-one.

362.title: What the role asks
362.hook: duties are measured by relationships: father, brother, neighbor (Enchiridion 30)
362.howItsDone: People who practice Stoicism often think through their roles, as child, parent, friend, neighbor or worker, and ask what each one asks of them, rather than what the other person has earned.

segments.voice: Yesterday: count the cost first, the athlete who looks at the whole training before signing up. Your line was first, what follows. Which plan did you count? Day three hundred sixty-two.

A student comes to Epictetus with a complaint that sounds airtight. My father is a bad father. Surely that changes what I owe him. It's a question people still bring to therapists, to clergy, to friends at two in the morning. And the handbook's thirtieth section answers it with a single short reply that has been argued over ever since. It doesn't start with feelings, or with fairness. It starts with a relationship, and asks what that relationship, on its own, asks of you. Today: what the role asks.
screen: `MY FATHER IS A BAD FATHER.` → `SURELY THAT CHANGES THINGS?` → `WHAT THE ROLE ASKS.`

segments.voice: First, the rule. Duties, Epictetus says, are measured by relationships. Is he a father? Then the role asks you to take care of him and to give way to him. But he's a bad father, says the student. Epictetus answers: were you tied by nature to a good father? No. To a father. Second, the brother. Your brother treats you unjustly. Then keep your own place toward him, Epictetus says. Don't watch what he is doing. Watch what you must do to keep your own choices in line with nature. And he adds his usual hinge: no one can harm you unless you allow it. Third, today's word. The Stoics called a fitting act kathēkon, the thing that is appropriate for this creature, in this place, in this relationship. The ancient biographer Diogenes Laertius says Zeno, the founder of the school, first used the term. Later Cicero turned it into Latin as officium, and wrote a whole book called On Duties around it. That Latin word is the far ancestor of our word office, a post with things you're expected to do. Fourth, the method. Epictetus says you'll find the duty of a neighbor, a citizen, a general, if you get used to looking at the relationship itself. Ask, what am I to this person, and the next step usually shows up. One honest caution. Epictetus wrote that a son should bear even blows from his father, in a world that took that for granted. Many modern readers of the Stoics add plainly that no role asks anyone to stay in danger, and protecting yourself is also a duty. What the chapter keeps is narrower: their failure doesn't erase your part.
screen: `DUTIES ARE MEASURED BY RELATIONSHIPS.` · `NOT A GOOD FATHER. A FATHER.` · `KATHĒKON: THE FITTING ACT.` · `ASK: WHAT AM I TO THIS PERSON?` · then, large: `WHAT THE ROLE ASKS.`

segments.voice: Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind the roles you hold this week. Child of someone. Friend. Neighbor. Coworker. Maybe parent, partner, sibling. Pick just one. Picture the person on the other side of it. Now ask Epictetus' question, quietly: what does this role ask of me today? Not what they deserve. Not what would be fair. What the role itself asks. Let one small answer come: a call, a dish washed, a word of thanks. Hold it. The bell holds the time.
Kathēkon. The Stoic word for the fitting act: what a role or relationship asks of you. Cicero called it officium, duty. Today's word.
Your line: what the role asks. Do one duty of one role today, the one that came to you in the sit, whether or not the other person notices. Day three hundred sixty-two.

363.title: Honor, simply
363.hook: Epictetus on reverence: think rightly of the gods and keep offerings honest and plain (Enchiridion 31)
363.howItsDone: Epictetus advised keeping the customary offerings of one's ancestors, plainly and within one's means; some people on their own path today keep a small, simple ritual for whatever they hold sacred.

segments.voice: Yesterday: kathēkon, the fitting act, measured by the relationship. Your line was what the role asks. Which duty did you do, and for whom? Day three hundred sixty-three.

A small clay cup of wine, poured out on the ground before a meal. A handful of the first barley of the harvest, set at a household shrine. In Epictetus' world, offerings like these belonged to ordinary household life, the way some families today light a candle, say grace, or leave flowers at a grave. The handbook doesn't skip over it. Section thirty-one is about reverence, and what's striking is how little it asks for. Two things. Think rightly. Give plainly. Today: honor, simply.
screen: `A CUP POURED ON THE GROUND.` → `THE FIRST BARLEY AT THE SHRINE.` → `HONOR, SIMPLY.`

segments.voice: First, the thinking. The most important part of piety, Epictetus says, is to hold right opinions about the gods: that they exist, and that they govern the whole well and justly. That's his belief, a Stoic's. People on their own path hold many different views here, and this lesson is about the shape of his advice more than the content of his creed. Second, why the thinking matters. Once you hold that view, he says, you can follow what happens willingly, and you'll never blame the gods. But only if you put good and bad in what's up to you. If you put them in outside things, then every time you miss what you wanted, you'll feel cheated, and you'll resent whoever you think is in charge. He gives a hard example from the old stories: Eteocles and Polynices, brothers who killed each other over the throne of Thebes, because each thought the crown was the good. Farmers, sailors and merchants complain at the sky for the same reason. Third, the giving. Pour the libations, make the offerings, give the first fruits, he says, according to the custom of your ancestors. And do it purely. Not carelessly. Not sloppily. Not stingily. And not beyond what you can afford. Fourth, why it travels. You may not share his gods, or any gods. Still, a person can hold something sacred: a faith, the memory of a grandmother, a mountain, a quiet morning. Epictetus' advice still fits. Don't make it a show, and don't let it go shabby. Honor it honestly, within your means, in the way you were given. Simple isn't the same as small.
screen: `FIRST: THINK RIGHTLY OF THE GODS.` · `MISPLACED GOOD BREEDS RESENTMENT.` · `NOT CARELESS, STINGY, OR TOO MUCH.` · `HONEST AND PLAIN, WHATEVER YOU HOLD.` · then, large: `HONESTLY, SIMPLY.`

segments.voice: Settle in, and breathe. Ask yourself what you hold sacred. It might be God, or a tradition, or a person who's gone, or the sea, or something you don't have a name for. Let one come to mind. Now picture a plain way to honor it today. Not a grand gesture. A candle lit. A minute of silence. A photo dusted. A walk to the water. If you pray, a prayer you already know. Choose one, and see yourself doing it, carefully and without fuss. The bell holds the time.
Honor. In Enchiridion thirty-one, reverence comes in two parts: right thinking, and offerings made honestly, plainly, and within your means. Today's word.
Your line: honestly, simply. Make one small, honest gesture toward what you hold sacred today, no bigger than it needs to be, and no smaller. Day three hundred sixty-three.

364.title: No oracle needed
364.hook: ask diviners about things you can't know, never about whether to stand by a friend (Enchiridion 32)
364.howItsDone: Some people who practice Stoicism separate questions about outcomes, which they may research or ask about, from questions about duty, which they try to answer by reason without waiting for a sign.

segments.voice: Yesterday: honor, and reverence in two parts, right thinking and plain giving. Your line was honestly, simply. What small gesture did you make? Day three hundred sixty-four.

The call comes after midnight. A friend is in trouble, and they need someone to come. It's a moment when a small voice can start bargaining. Is this a good idea? Maybe I should sleep on it. Maybe I'll wait and see how I feel in the morning. People in Epictetus' day had a more formal way to stall. They went to a diviner, someone who read birds or the insides of a sacrifice, and asked what the gods advised. Epictetus doesn't mock the diviner. He just draws a line around what the diviner is for. Today: no oracle needed.
screen: `A FRIEND IN TROUBLE, LATE AT NIGHT.` → `ASK THE DIVINER?` → `NO ORACLE NEEDED.`

segments.voice: First, how to walk in. When you go to a diviner, Epictetus says, you don't know how things will turn out. That's why you came. But you do know what kind of thing it is. If it isn't up to you, it isn't good or bad in itself. So leave your craving and your dread at the door, and go in the way you'd go to any adviser. Second, when to ask. Go the way Socrates went, he says: only when the whole question turns on what will happen, and reason and skill have nothing to offer. Will a voyage go well? Will a harvest come in? Questions like those, fine. Third, when not to ask. When a friend or your country is in danger and you ought to share it, don't ask the diviner whether to. Even if the signs say death, injury or exile, reason has already answered. You stand by your friend. Fourth, the greater diviner. Epictetus tells an old story about the god at Delphi, who, it was said, threw a man out of the temple because he had not helped a friend who was being killed. Even the oracle, in the story, sides with loyalty over omens. And a look back at the week, since today closes it: these things happen. Aim at the good. My mind is mine. First, what follows. What the role asks. Honestly, simply. And today, a duty doesn't wait for a sign.

segments.voice: Sit comfortably, and breathe. Think of one duty you've been putting off while you wait for some kind of sign. The right mood. A clearer feeling. Someone else going first. Maybe it's a call, a visit, an apology, an offer of help. Look at it plainly. Is this a question about what will happen, or about what you owe? If it's what you owe, the answer may already be in your hands. Let the waiting go, and picture the first step. The bell holds the time.
No oracle needed. When the question is whether to stand by a friend, Epictetus says, reason has already answered. Today's word.
